Everyone in the comments seems to question why Ashar having concerns regarding Khirad and Khijar. Everyone's saying that it's hypocritical of him cause he himself has a female friend. Which is fair, I am not gonna dismiss this argument. It has its ground. But I would like to add somethings. I think his problem isn't Khirad having a male friend, it's khizar's behavior that is bothering him and the fact that Khirad is not understanding or overlooking khizar's behavior or she's just thinking that khizar is being friendly. Which is again not her fault completely. The main culprit here is Khizar here. Ashar's concerns are regarding him and the way he's crossing boundaries, which is not right! And the fact that Khirad is a simplistic girl, as the show heavily implies that she's a masoom and very kind hearted woman. Which is totally fine and not wrong at all! But people tend to take advantage of such people, use them, exploit them in a way that ruin their life, family, relationships everything etc.! And Ashar's concern gains more ground as he is constantly heard from his father, mother, people around him and he also genuinely believes that Khirad is a masoom and kind hearted woman! Again which is not wrong to be masoom and kind hearted, but his concerns is that her this masoomiyat and kind heartiness is not letting her see through the actual motives and intentions of Khizar! And he is concern that khizar might use Khirad! Which can lead up to catastrophic consequences. It might not always be the case that a man doesn't trust his wife, but the fact that he as man knows what other man are like! Which some women might fail to see behind all the sweet impressions and stuffs! So his concerns are genuinely valid, please try to understand this. And regarding the hypocrisy part, yes he himself had female friend, but there are somethings to clear up! First of all I am a firm believer on the fact that a man and a woman cannot ever be just friends, one will always want to be more than that. And it's the case of majority! So in my framework both are wrong here to keep male/female friends or even interact with opposite gender frankly or in a way that might give the other person wrong impression. Sure your intentions were clear, but the other person's interpretation of your intentions might not be! So in my personal opinion and framework, both Ashar and Khirad are wrong to keep friends of opposite gender respectively. Even tho Khirad is not keeping khizar as her friend, but he heavily insists on that, which is his problem as I said earlier about intentions and interpretation. Khirad is just being a nice person where as khizar is interpreting it in a wrong way! Again which is his problem. So Khirad is really has the edge when it comes to who is closer to being right. I am insisting on these points to clear up that I am not here to take sides, not Ashar's nor Khirad. And I am here also not to justify any wrong behavior of Ashar, I am just trying give valid reasons and concerns why as of this point in the series Ashar is concerned. So now I will talk outside of my framework, so regarding Ashar and Sara's friendship we have to understand that their friendship is long before Ashar and Khirad's marriage. They're childhood friends! Their friendship really has a much more strong ground than Khirad and khizar's! Ashar just can't suddenly stop being friends with Sara out of nowhere! So saying that Ashar is a hypocrite purely based on this criteria that he's friends with Sara is not completely justified imo if we keep my own framework outside and talk from a different,more liberal perspective. And one other thing is that Khirad's constant mention of Khizar in front of Ashar. Which is not right, we didn't see Ashar doing that around with Khirad, constantly mentioning Sara. Khirad maybe doing this unknowingly but it's still doesn't sit right with him, in fact it will not with any spouse respectively! And the other thing is Khizar's constant involvement in Khirad's life and his family which is affecting himself! And his relationship with Khirad! His unusual interest in Khirad's life, coming out of nowhere in their house, being so frank with Khirad doesn't sit right with him! On top of that when Khirad keeps bringing khizar into conversation it really bother's him. Yes he should confront khizar about all these and this is where I will say he's wrong! Instead of confronting the actual culprit he shouldn't make assumptions that can lead up to something horrible! And this is a legit criticism! And we should talk about tthis! I kept wondering, “Can something really happen in a drama that will make the heroine suffer this much? Will Ashar and Khirad actually separate?”

I never imagined that Farida had been planning everything from the very beginning. She hated Khirad from the start but never let anyone understand what she really felt. Her acting was so convincing. Later, she teamed up with Zarina and Khizr and created a whole conspiracy to make Khirad look bad in front of Ashar.

What kind of mother does that to her own son? She literally destroyed her own son's life. Everything was going perfectly until Farida ruined it all. If she hadn't done what she did, Sara would probably have gotten married by now instead of waiting all those years for Ashar. And in the end, Sara died. She didn't have to die either. 😭

Ashar is actually a good man. He trusted his mother, and honestly, how could he ever imagine that his own mother was capable of doing something like this? Yes, he was wrong for not believing Khirad, but he loved her so deeply. 💔

And honestly, I'm glad Farida went crazy in the end. She deserved it after everything she did. 😭

Asher probably never knew failure in his life. As a rich, good-looking kid, things likely came easily to him. He was content as long as he remained the center of Khirad’s world. When she began studying and building a life beyond him, he seemed to grow insecure. His mother noticed this and later exploited it to drive a wedge between them.

His shock at finding Khirad in a compromising situation with another man is understandable, but his reaction was absolutely not. He knew Khirad was principled and brutally honest, so why he didn’t even give her a chance to explain is something I’ll never understand. What makes it worse is that he was perceptive enough to see through Sara’s fake kindness and even call it out. Yet with Khirad - the woman he claimed to love - he showed no such discernment. His wounded ego and fear of humiliation completely blinded him.

None of this justifies the injustice he inflicted on Khirad. His real punishment is having to live with the knowledge that he failed both his wife and daughter. Even if they move forward, neither of them will ever forget these four years. Khirad returned only because of their child, and while they may build a life together again, I feel the essence of their relationship was permanently lost.

The drama was absolutely amazing, and almost every episode was enjoyable until Shamir and Shibra got married. After their marriage, the story somehow felt different, and the quality of the episodes was not as strong as before.

However, all of the actors did a fantastic job portraying their characters. The character of Fazal Baksh was especially entertaining. He was incredibly funny, and his dialogues were outstanding. Many of his scenes made the drama even more enjoyable.

The earlier episodes were truly mind-blowing and kept me hooked from the beginning. The story, suspense, and character development were excellent. Unfortunately, I don’t think the ending lived up to the standard set by the earlier episodes. While the drama as a whole was still very good, the finale could have been written and executed much better.

Overall, it was a wonderful drama with memorable characters, great performances, and many unforgettable moments, but the ending was not as satisfying as I had hoped.

I didn’t like the way Shamir’s relationship with his father-in-law was handled in the last moments of the story. From the beginning of the drama, Mr. Suleman and Shamir shared a very strong bond. In fact, Shamir didn’t even seem to have such a close relationship with his own father. Mr. Suleman cared for him like his own son, hugged him, gave him a place in his home, and treated him as part of the family.

I understand that Shamir wanted to protect his political party, but he could have at least visited Mr. Suleman in jail, even secretly. At the very least, he should not have spoken those words in front of the media. Shamir knew that his father-in-law was innocent, yet he did not have the courage to tell the truth publicly. How can he be a leader of justice if he cannot stand up for an innocent man?

I think if Shamir’s mother had still been alive, she would have had the courage to openly declare that Mr. Suleman was innocent. She never cared about public opinion when it came to doing the right thing, and that was why people respected her as a leader of justice.

I know politics is not easy, but throughout the drama politicians were shown to have the power to get people released from jail with a single phone call. Yet Shamir could do absolutely nothing for the man who treated him like a son. In the end, Mr. Suleman died, and Shamir did not even investigate what had really happened. How could a man simply die or suicide  in jail without anyone looking into it?

Another thing I disliked was that Shamir barely showed any emotion after Mr. Suleman’s death. One of the reasons Shamir loved Shibra was because of her honesty and kindness. He valued her character more than her beauty. In the same way, he should have admired and respected his father-in-law even more. After Mr. Suleman’s death, Shamir should have been deeply emotional and regretful, realizing that his own mistakes had cost him such a noble man.

He failed to protect him. At the very least, he should have felt guilty for putting Mr. Suleman in such a vulnerable position. Giving an honest officer a major role in fighting corruption could naturally make him a target of false accusations. Why didn’t Shamir take precautions earlier? Why didn’t he visit him in jail with Shibra during the final episodes?

There were also some inconsistencies in the last episodes. Mehrin threatened Shibra, yet Shibra never told Shamir about it. Even after being attacked, she never seriously suspected Mehrin or mentioned her name. Similarly, Mr. Suleman was told that Shibra’s life could be in danger, yet he never informed Shamir about it. These plot points made the final episodes feel disconnected from the rest of the drama.

Mr. Suleman was an honest man, and I am glad that he was eventually proven innocent. However, I think it would have been even more meaningful if the drama had emphasized that he remained honest throughout his entire life and that, because of his integrity, Allah honored him by revealing the truth in the end. That would have delivered a powerful message: if a person remains truthful and honest throughout life, they will earn respect and honor even after death.

Ishq Murshid — Review 🇧🇩

Just finished Ishq Murshid, and honestly, I really enjoyed the journey. Shahmeer and Shibra were the heart of the drama. Bilal Abbas Khan did an amazing job portraying both Shahmeer and Fazal Bakhsh—the contrast between his serious, intelligent personality and Fazal Bakhsh’s innocent, funny side was one of the best things about the drama. Durefishan Saleem was equally impressive as Shibra, and their chemistry felt natural and enjoyable throughout.

I also liked the supporting characters, especially Zubaida and Safdar Shah, because they added more depth to the family and political side of the story. The drama had a good mix of romance, comedy, emotions and mystery, and the characters kept me interested for most of the journey.

My biggest disappointment was the ending. Everything suddenly moved way too fast, and it honestly felt like several important parts of the story were skipped or rushed. Some characters and conflicts deserved a proper conclusion instead of being wrapped up so quickly.

Overall, Ishq Murshid was a beautiful and entertaining watch with great performances and memorable characters. I just wish the writers had given the ending more time and depth.

8/10 ❤️🇧🇩

The drama shows the hero following the ideals of his mother, who was an honest leader trying to run the country with integrity. On the other hand, the heroine also shares similar values. Everything builds toward a strong message of honest leadership and commitment.

However, in the end, the hero fails to handle the party and decides to step away from leadership. This feels inconsistent. Throughout the drama, he is inspired by his mother’s ideals, and even in his imagination, she encourages him to carry forward her vision. But ultimately, he gives up, which contradicts that entire buildup.

Because of this, the ending doesn’t feel satisfying or meaningful. It raises the question—what was the actual message of the drama?

In many societies, married women continue to face numerous challenges when they attempt to pursue professional careers. Although modernization and education have created new opportunities, traditional mindsets still restrict women’s growth and independence. In many families, married women are discouraged—or even prohibited—from working outside the home. Deeply rooted cultural beliefs often define men as the primary breadwinners, while women are expected to manage domestic responsibilities. If a woman contributes financially or earns more than her husband, it may be viewed as inappropriate or threatening. Such attitudes not only limit women’s opportunities but also affect their confidence and sense of self-worth.

Even when married women are permitted to work, balancing professional responsibilities with household duties becomes a major challenge. In most cases, domestic work and childcare remain primarily the woman’s responsibility, regardless of her employment status. This “double burden” leaves women physically exhausted and emotionally strained. The expectation that they must excel both at home and at work creates constant pressure. Without shared responsibilities from spouses or family members, maintaining this equilibrium becomes nearly impossible.

Married working women also encounter significant challenges in the workplace. Many organizations expect employees to work late hours or remain available beyond official timings. For women with children and household obligations, such demands can be difficult to fulfill. The lack of supportive workplace policies, such as flexible hours or remote work options, further complicates the situation. Additionally, the absence of facilities like daycare centers or nurseries forces mothers to rely on relatives or costly childcare services. This ongoing stress affects their productivity and overall job satisfaction.

Another serious issue is workplace discrimination. In some professional environments, women are not taken as seriously as their male counterparts. Harmful stereotypes suggest that women are less capable, less committed, or hired merely to improve the office atmosphere rather than for their skills. Such biased attitudes lower morale and discourage women from fully participating in professional growth opportunities. The lack of mentorship and social support from colleagues and supervisors can result in absenteeism, reduced confidence, and higher turnover rates. Therefore, management and higher authorities must create inclusive workplaces where merit and competence are valued above gender.

Transportation is another major obstacle, especially in developing countries. Public transport systems are often overcrowded, unreliable, and unsafe. While these conditions affect everyone, women face the additional risk of harassment during travel. Due to financial limitations, many working women depend on buses or vans instead of private transport. Fear of unsafe travel conditions creates anxiety and, in some cases, forces women to resign from their jobs. Governments must prioritize improving public transportation systems and enforcing strict safety measures to ensure secure travel for women.

Despite these challenges, women across the world continue to demonstrate resilience and determination. Self-confidence and continuous skill development are essential tools for overcoming obstacles. In the digital age, online education and professional training platforms offer countless opportunities for growth. Women can enhance their technical expertise, strengthen communication skills, and expand professional networks. As Michelle Obama wisely stated, “There is no limit to what we, as women, can accomplish.” This powerful message highlights the boundless potential women possess when given equal opportunities.

Education and awareness are equally important in transforming societal attitudes. Men and society as a whole must learn to respect women not only as family members but as independent individuals with ambitions and rights. Malala Yousafzai emphasizes this collective responsibility: “I raise up my voice—not so that I can shout, but so that those without a voice can be heard... We cannot all succeed when half of us are held back.” Her words remind us that true progress is impossible when women are restricted or silenced.

Furthermore, leadership and advocacy play a crucial role in promoting gender equality. Melinda French Gates states, “A woman with a voice is, by definition, a strong woman.” Empowering women to speak up and participate in decision-making processes strengthens not only individuals but entire communities. Similarly, Elizabeth Nyamayaro explains, “Gender equality is not a woman's issue, it is a human rights issue. It affects us all.” This perspective reinforces the idea that equality benefits society as a whole, not just women.

Ultimately, the journey of a married woman toward professional fulfillment is not an individual struggle but a shared responsibility. Governments must ensure safe transportation and enforce protective laws. Corporations should implement family-friendly policies and promote equal opportunities. Within families, partners must share domestic responsibilities to create balance and mutual respect. When artificial barriers are removed, women can contribute fully to economic growth and social development. By fostering supportive environments and progressive thinking, societies can empower married working women and build a more equitable future for generations to come.

In many societies, married women continue to face numerous challenges when they attempt to pursue professional careers. Although modernization and education have created new opportunities, traditional mindsets still restrict women’s growth and independence. In many families, married women are discouraged—or even prohibited—from working outside the home. Deeply rooted cultural beliefs often define men as the primary breadwinners, while women are expected to manage domestic responsibilities. If a woman contributes financially or earns more than her husband, it may be viewed as inappropriate or threatening. Such attitudes not only limit women’s opportunities but also affect their confidence and sense of self-worth.

Even when married women are permitted to work, balancing professional responsibilities with household duties becomes a major challenge. In most cases, domestic work and childcare remain primarily the woman’s responsibility, regardless of her employment status. This “double burden” leaves women physically exhausted and emotionally strained. The expectation that they must excel both at home and at work creates constant pressure. Without shared responsibilities from spouses or family members, maintaining this equilibrium becomes nearly impossible.

Married working women also encounter significant challenges in the workplace. Many organizations expect employees to work late hours or remain available beyond official timings. For women with children and household obligations, such demands can be difficult to fulfill. The lack of supportive workplace policies, such as flexible hours or remote work options, further complicates the situation. Additionally, the absence of facilities like daycare centers or nurseries forces mothers to rely on relatives or costly childcare services. This ongoing stress affects their productivity and overall job satisfaction.

Another serious issue is workplace discrimination. In some professional environments, women are not taken as seriously as their male counterparts. Harmful stereotypes suggest that women are less capable, less committed, or hired merely to improve the office atmosphere rather than for their skills. Such biased attitudes lower morale and discourage women from fully participating in professional growth opportunities. The lack of mentorship and social support from colleagues and supervisors can result in absenteeism, reduced confidence, and higher turnover rates. Therefore, management and higher authorities must create inclusive workplaces where merit and competence are valued above gender.

Transportation is another major obstacle, especially in developing countries. Public transport systems are often overcrowded, unreliable, and unsafe. While these conditions affect everyone, women face the additional risk of harassment during travel. Due to financial limitations, many working women depend on buses or vans instead of private transport. Fear of unsafe travel conditions creates anxiety and, in some cases, forces women to resign from their jobs. Governments must prioritize improving public transportation systems and enforcing strict safety measures to ensure secure travel for women.

Despite these challenges, women across the world continue to demonstrate resilience and determination. Self-confidence and continuous skill development are essential tools for overcoming obstacles. In the digital age, online education and professional training platforms offer countless opportunities for growth. Women can enhance their technical expertise, strengthen communication skills, and expand professional networks. As Michelle Obama wisely stated, “There is no limit to what we, as women, can accomplish.” This powerful message highlights the boundless potential women possess when given equal opportunities.

Education and awareness are equally important in transforming societal attitudes. Men and society as a whole must learn to respect women not only as family members but as independent individuals with ambitions and rights. Malala Yousafzai emphasizes this collective responsibility: “I raise up my voice—not so that I can shout, but so that those without a voice can be heard... We cannot all succeed when half of us are held back.” Her words remind us that true progress is impossible when women are restricted or silenced.

Furthermore, leadership and advocacy play a crucial role in promoting gender equality. Melinda French Gates states, “A woman with a voice is, by definition, a strong woman.” Empowering women to speak up and participate in decision-making processes strengthens not only individuals but entire communities. Similarly, Elizabeth Nyamayaro explains, “Gender equality is not a woman's issue, it is a human rights issue. It affects us all.” This perspective reinforces the idea that equality benefits society as a whole, not just women.

Ultimately, the journey of a married woman toward professional fulfillment is not an individual struggle but a shared responsibility. Governments must ensure safe transportation and enforce protective laws. Corporations should implement family-friendly policies and promote equal opportunities. Within families, partners must share domestic responsibilities to create balance and mutual respect. When artificial barriers are removed, women can contribute fully to economic growth and social development. By fostering supportive environments and progressive thinking, societies can empower married working women and build a more equitable future for generations to come.

🔖 I really liked the drama Farizaad from the beginning. Every episode touched my heart—especially the character of the hero. It was so realistic and emotional that it often brought tears to my eyes. But no… towards the end, especially episodes 28 to 30 — I found them completely disappointing. I couldn’t enjoy them at all. I never imagined such a beautiful story would end in such a disheartening way.

I thought Farizaad would get married, and the story would have a happy ending. Something to comfort the audience who cried through all the painful moments. But instead, it ended in a way that felt like sorrow itself was the only gift we were given. Now it feels like all the emotions I invested, all the tears I shed — were all for nothing.

It’s okay to create stories inspired by real life, but ending them in a way that breaks the audience’s heart is just not right. Now I feel like watching the entire drama was a waste of time. I have a playlist saved with 10–15 Pakistani dramas — I’m going to unsave them all. If all dramas end like this, then it's not worth watching. Like I’ve stopped watching Indian dramas, I might have to give up Pakistani dramas too.

We, the audience, look for a little happiness at the end of a story — a bit of hope. And when we don’t get that, it makes us realize this story was never meant for us, never meant to win our hearts.

Do din aur do raatein lagatar sirf ek hi ehsaas mein dooba raha—'Parizaad'. 30 episodes ka yeh safar kab meri rooh ke andar tak utar gaya, pata hi nahi chala. Kya bemisaal qalam thi Hashim Nadeem sahab ki, kya jaanleva adakari thi Ahmed Ali Akbar ki, aur kya lajawab hidayat-kari (direction).

Ek writer aur director hone ke naate shayad main har kirdar ke dard, khamoshi aur thehrav ko kuch zyada hi gehraai se mehsoos kar gaya. Jab koi audience kisi kahani se dil se judti hai, toh woh sirf tamasha nahi dekh rahi hoti, woh kahin na kahin khud ko us kirdar ki jagah rakh kar jee rahi hoti hai.

Shuruat se lekar aakhir tak bas yahi ek aas, yahi ek umeed bandhi rahi ki shayad is bebas, paak aur saaf dil rooh ko woh mohabbat mil jaye jo chehron aur daulat se pare sirf rooh se ki jaati hai. Poori duniya ki zillat sehne ke baad dil bas itna chahta tha ki kaash uska anjaam thoda aur pursukoon aur khushnuma hota. Yeh khaalipan aur dil ki udaasi shayad bohot lambe waqt tak seene mein bhaari rahegi.

Aakhir mein, meri taraf se Hashim Nadeem sahab, director Shahzad Kashmiri sahab, Ahmed Ali Akbar aur poori team ko teh-e-dil se bohot bohot mubarakbaad. Aap sab ne jis shiddat, lagan aur be-panah mehnat ke saath is master-piece ko banaya hai, uska nateeja waqai lajawab aur tareekhi hai.

Parizaad sirf ek drama nahi, balki insani jazbaat aur tanhai ka woh aaina hai jise bhool pana mumkin nahi. Hats off to the entire team!

As an audience member, watching Parizaad felt like an emotional journey that completely changed what I expect from television. Unlike typical dramas that focus on glitz, wealth, and toxic romance, this story stays with you because of how purely human and gentle the main character is.
Ahmed Ali Akbar didn't just play a role; he made you feel every ounce of Parizaad’s pain, rejection, and quiet resilience. It was heartbreaking to watch society judge him just because of his skin color and humble background, yet inspiring to see that success and money never corrupted his golden heart. The dynamic with RJ Annie and the raw, poetry-filled moments brought tears to my eyes more than once.
The ending was unconventional and refreshing—instead of a loud, predictable conclusion, seeing him find peace in simplicity felt like the healing closure he deserved. It is a rare masterpiece that makes you look at people with more empathy.

Conclusion

Meerab is a genuinely stubborn and bemusing character. It's perplexing to observe her thought processes and actions throughout this drama. While her role is ostensibly that of the protagonist, she consistently presents herself as the show's antagonist.
Consider the unwavering devotion she receives
Murtasim’s unconditional love, her parents' affection, and even her mother in law, who is not nearly as bad as Meerab makes her out to be. One could argue that Haya is not a character to be defended she is as manipulative as Rohail.
Yet, despite this network of support from Anwar, Waqas, her mother, and Murtasim all of whom protect and accommodate her Meerab appears entirely undeserving of such loyalty. In fact, one could argue that Murtasim deserves far better.
Some may disagree with this perspective, but I would ask them to truly put themselves in Murtasim’s position. He did not force her into this marriage on the contrary, he explicitly confirmed her consent twice. She, however, entered into it seemingly with the sole intention of punishing him and ensuring the marriage would fail, all while actively pursuing a connection with Rohail.
While she is constantly shielded and forgiven by those around her, she rarely, if ever, extends the same grace or protection in return
She comes across as deeply ironic and hypocritical, a character primarily concerned with her own interests and driven by a desire for revenge on her own terms.

Ultimately, it feels as though the writer has gone to great lengths to craft a protagonist who is as deeply flawed and frustrating as possible

Meerab is an ambitious and beautiful young girl who wants to pursue higher studies. Her entire world revolves around her parents and she believes in them the most. Her strong and confident personality makes her stand against social injustices around her.

On the contrary, Murtasim hails from a powerful and influential family. He respects and values the morals and traditions of his family and refuses to let the family down.

Meerab’s life takes an unexpected turn when she finds out about her family’s decision regarding her and Murtasim’s life. Meerab’s hatred towards Murtasim continues to grow as a family secret from the past resurfaces. Coming from different backgrounds and mindsets, Murtasim begins to realize Meerab’s arrogant behaviour towards him and begins to consider her a challenge for himself. On the other hand, Meerab who is used to living her life on her own terms refuses to accept Murtasim’s family traditions and unnecessary social barriers.

Soon their lives go through a series of emotional sufferings and misunderstandings where it becomes difficult for them to coexist. Despite their hatred towards each other, will Meerab and Murtasim accept their true feelings or will the dynamics of ego and self-respect force them to stay apart?

-The wording of the agreement itself and constant undertones in tge story promotes marital rape and abuse. A big thank you to the writers, producers, and everyone who worked hard to bring this beautiful drama to life and give us such enjoyable and memorable scenes. Honestly, the drama ended at a perfect point, and I think it would have been difficult to give it a better ending.

I especially loved Haya’s ending because she played a negative character in the drama. Meرب’s arrival at Haya and Murtasim’s nikah, along with Haya’s disappointment, helplessness, and sense of defeat, was such a satisfying scene. From her expression and reaction, it felt as though she had lost everything. To be honest, I really enjoyed seeing Haya face the consequences of her actions. Sometimes, watching a negative character experience the outcome of their own choices brings a certain satisfaction.

I wish Maryam had returned too and been there to share in the happiness of Murtasim and Meerab finally coming together. ❤

And that final scene, where Meerab wipes away Murtasim’s tears, was absolutely heart-melting! ❤‍🩹 So much love, compassion, and emotion were expressed through such a small gesture. It was more than just wiping away tears; it felt as though Meerab truly understood Murtasim’s pain and wanted to comfort him without saying a word. Not everyone can understand another person’s pain so deeply or ease the burden on someone’s heart in such a beautiful way.

Some scenes stay in your mind long after a drama ends, and for me, that final moment between Meerab and Murtasim was one of them.

Overall, my heartfelt thanks to the entire team for bringing such a beautiful story to an end in this way. Some dramas are simply watched to pass the time, but others leave us with emotions that stay with us long after the final scene. ❤
